title: Microburst reserve & spot-mix simulation notes
content:
Purpose:
This working note captures a simulation we ran exploring a mixed capacity strategy for Hosted API: combining reserved capacity (commit/slots) with ephemeral spot-style instances (burst/spot pools) to handle short, high-percentile microbursts while optimizing unit economics and margin. The focus is on 95–99.9th percentile request bursts that dominate peak GPU slot needs but are infrequent enough that a blended spot/reserve approach may reduce average COGS.

High-level hypothesis:
- Carving out a small reserved baseline for steady-state demand and routing microbursts to a spot/burst tier can materially reduce amortized per-token COGS without degrading 95–99.5% tail latency if fallback and routing policies are tuned.
- The net benefit depends on model family (decoder vs chat), regional spot availability, and sequence-length profile (longer sequences favor reserve).

Assumptions (input to sim):
- Time granularity: 1-minute bins over a 30-day trace sampled from production (regional split: us-west, us-east, eu-west).
- Baseline steady slots per region derived from 50th percentile minute load.
- Microburst classification: bursts where minute demand > baseline * 3. Microbursts occur on average 4% of minutes, concentrated in business hours and product launches.
- Reserved slots: paid monthly amortized rate = $2.20/slot-hour (includes infra + license amortization).
- Spot/burst slot assumed hourly equivalent price = $0.95/slot-hour but with 12% reclamation probability per hour (workload must gracefully handle interruptions).
- Slot throughput converted to tokens using model family effective tokens/sec: small-decoder=2000 tokens/s per slot, chat-encoder=1200 tokens/s (includes attention and tooling overhead), long-context-optim = 1500 tokens/s for 8k models.
- KV-cache and prefix caching reduce token load during repeated prompts: two profiles simulated (cache-hit-rate 30% vs 60%).
- SLO constraints: 95th latency target 300ms, 99th latency target 600ms. Microburst routing must keep 99th <= 600ms; otherwise additional reserve required.

Simulation scenarios run (representative):
1) Baseline all-reserve: reserve enough slots to satisfy 99th percentile minute demand (no spot).
2) Small-reserve + spot-burst: reserve = 60th percentile demand, spot covers bursts above baseline at 0.95$/slot-hr with reclamation and 2-second cold-start penalty on pre-warming if slot not ready; fallback to queued short jobs if reclamation occurs.
3) Conservative hybrid (reserve = 80th percentile) + spot for extreme peaks only.
4) Region-aware mix: higher reserve in regions with less spot availability (eu-west reserve factor +10%), leverage more spot in us-west.

Key simulation outputs (summary):
- Metric: amortized per-1k tokens COGS, 95/99 latency percentiles, monthly cost variance, reclamation-induced retries, and margin delta vs baseline pricing.

Example aggregated results (30-day trace, weighted across models):
- Scenario 1 (all-reserve): per-1k tokens COGS = $0.0185; 95/99 latency = 180ms / 420ms; monthly infra cost = $1,210,000; margin at list price = 42%.
- Scenario 2 (60/spot): per-1k tokens COGS = $0.0139 (-25%); 95/99 latency = 210ms / 470ms; monthly infra cost = $945,000 (-22%); reclamation events = 1.4% of spot-hours; observed retried requests = 0.09% of total tokens (retries increased tail by ~10% relative to baseline).
- Scenario 3 (80/spot): per-1k tokens COGS = $0.0161 (-13%); 95/99 latency = 190ms / 435ms; monthly infra cost = $1,060,000 (-12%); reclamation events = 0.8% of spot-hours.
- Scenario 4 (region-aware): per-1k tokens COGS = $0.0146 (-21%); 95/99 latency = 200ms / 460ms; monthly infra cost = $995,000 (-18%); shows best balance for mixed geography.

Observations and sensitivity notes:
- The biggest driver of realized savings is burst frequency and length. If bursts are short (< 3 minutes) and infrequent, spot mix has outsized benefit. If bursts are long or sustained, the amortization advantage of reserve grows and spot becomes less favorable.
- Sequence length and model family matter: long-context models (higher tokens/req) erode spot benefit because a single reclaimed slot forces expensive retries or downgrade to smaller models.
- Cache-hit-rate strongly amplifies savings; when cache hits increase (60%), effective token load declines meaning spot pools handle bursts more cheaply.
- Reclamation/retry cost model: we assumed retried requests get re-enqueued to reserve or another spot instance; this adds CPU and networking overhead and some user-visible latency — we modeled retry token overhead = 1.05x original.
- Cold-start penalties for spin-up of spot pools/scheduler path affect the 95th percentile more than the 99th because reclamation/retries inflate the tail. Pre-warming heuristics reduce cold-start but increase spot cost slightly.

Operational considerations and routing logic (draft):
- Baseline sizing: compute reserved baseline per model family and region as max(steady-state 60th percentile, min-reserve-floor set by SLA customers).
- Burst detection: detect minute-level surge > baseline*3 and route new requests to spot-burst queue; mark low-latency short requests (<= 512 tokens) as preferred for spot to minimize retry penalty.
- Pre-warm policy: when regional minute demand shows a sustained ramp (consecutive minute growth > 20%), trigger a 5-minute pre-warm of a small spot pool to reduce cold-start latency.
- Reclamation fallback: on spot reclaim, attempt soft-fallback to reserve pool; if reserve full, apply graceful degradation (truncate response, suggest shorter responses) for eligible endpoints, otherwise queue with backpressure.
- Admission control: strict token budget per request to enforce retry/cost limits; long-context requests receive reservation priority by default unless explicit opt-in to spot burst.

Quantitative recommendations (short list):
- Pilot 60% baseline reserve + spot burst mix in us-west and us-east for non-long-context models; target reduction ~20–25% per-token COGS.
- Keep EU regions more conservative (80% baseline) until spot reliability tests reach <0.5% reclamation.
- Implement opt-in request tag for \"spot-eligible\" so customers with cost-sensitivity can accept lower tail SLOs in exchange for cheaper pricing tiers.
- Add cache-awareness into routing: increase spot routing for session types with >50% cache-hit rate.

Risks and open questions:
- Regulatory / compliance: some enterprise customers may not accept execution on spot instances; need per-tenant controls and clear contract language.
- Accounting complexity: accurate attribution of retried token overhead to customer billing vs infra cost must be decided.
- UX / SLAs: potential for confusing customer experience if tail latency fluctuates; product needs transparent tiering and opt-in for cost-oriented lanes.
- Spot provider behavior can change quickly; run ongoing monitoring and automated rollback if reclamation > threshold.

Next steps / experiments (actionable):
- Run a 2-week canary in us-west with 10% of traffic marked spot-eligible (non long-context) and full telemetry on reclamation, retries, and end-to-end latency. Owner: Diego Martinez.
- Build a lightweight cost-allocator notebook that attributes retried token cost to conservative vs spot buckets to validate accounting assumptions. Owner: Priya Raman.
- Product: draft customer-facing opt-in SKU language + console flag for \"cost tier: spot-friendly\". Owner: Lena Novak.

Appendix: quick thought-experiment calc (back-of-envelope)
- If average token rate = 1.6k tokens/sec/slot and average request sizes are 200 tokens, a reclaimed 1-minute spot interruption that causes a 2x retry adds ~400 tokens worth of cost per impacted request. At list price $0.03/1k tokens this is $0.012 per impacted request in revenue; in contrast infra reclaim cost is borne on the infra side. Modeling these small deltas at scale is what makes per-token COGS sensitive to reclamation rate.

Notes / TODOs:
- Need richer modeling for multi-model priority lanes and for function calling tool hot-paths (where retries are expensive).
- Wire up region-specific spot reliability telemetry into Optimize dashboards.
- Follow up with legal on acceptable language for spot-execution in enterprise agreements.

End of working note.
